title: Breckenridge Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Breckenridge wells have a 135 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $14,800-$25,500.
h1: Breckenridge Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Breckenridge means dealing with mountain bedrock, limited well records, and site conditions that can change from one parcel to the next. Within five miles of Breckenridge, Colorado DWR records show 3,528 permitted wells. Of those, 1,948 are recorded as constructed, 2,261 report a total depth, and 1,234 report a pump yield.

The local records point to a typical domestic well in fractured granite or gneiss, not a predictable shallow alluvial well. The numbers below are useful for planning and comparing bids, but a nearby well is not a guarantee for your lot. Confirm the permit, construction record, water rights, septic layout, and access conditions before closing.

sections.heading: Breckenridge well depth reflects fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Breckenridge is 135 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 207 feet, while the 90th percentile is 290 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 1,000 feet. More than half of reported wells, 57%, fall between 100 and 300 feet; 34% are under 100 feet, and 9% are between 300 and 600 feet.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 3,481 wells in that category. That geology is the main reason depth can vary sharply across short distances. For a drilling bid, use the 135-foot median as a planning reference, not a promised refusal point. A parcel near Blue River or Keystone may still encounter different fractures, overburden, access, or casing conditions.

sections.heading: Local well yields are usually usable, but not uniform
sections.html:
Among the 1,234 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half falls between 8.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 26% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 8% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute; none of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

That distribution is encouraging for ordinary household use, but a pump test still matters. Yield is not the same as storage in the well, and a good short test does not answer every seasonal question. Ask for the well construction and yield records for the property and nearby wells in Frisco, Dillon, or Copper Mountain. Exempt household-use wells also have legal limits, including the 35 gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Breckenridge water levels vary by measurement decade
sections.html:
The median static water level is 80 feet below the ground surface, with the middle half from 45 to 120 feet. The decade medians are 75 feet in the 1970s, 80 feet in the 1980s, 70 feet in the 1990s, 95 feet in the 2000s, 70 feet in the 2010s, and 100 feet in the 2020s.

Only 288 wells report a static water level, so this is a limited sample. The series does not show a simple, steady decline: measurements move shallower and deeper across decades, with the 2020s median deeper than the 2010s. Treat that as a reason to inspect the individual well record and seasonal conditions, not as proof that the entire Breckenridge water table is dropping.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long local drilling activity
sections.html:
Breckenridge has a long well-permit record, with permits issued as far back as the 1960s and the newest permit year listed as 2025. The largest decade was the 1990s, with 1,006 permits. Records show 728 in the 2000s, 380 in the 2010s, and 273 in the 2020s. Use is predominantly domestic or household at 86%; monitoring accounts for 9%, and irrigation for 1%.

The most frequently listed drillers are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, Shelton, Joe Wayne, with 688 records; Buena Vista Drilling, Shelton, William L, with 469; and Arrow Drilling Co., Berglund, Paul R., with 285. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Verify licensing, insurance, references, and the exact scope of any proposal.

sections.heading: What a Breckenridge well can cost to drill
sections.html:
Local ground is fractured mountain bedrock, described in the cost model as granite or gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 135-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $8,800 to $13,500. That figure is only the drilling portion and should not be treated as the complete water-system budget.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,800 to $25,500 at the median depth. A bid can move outside that range if the hole is deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs more extensive trenching. Have the contractor state what is included and what happens if the hole is dry or requires additional depth.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying a mountain lot
sections.html:
Fractured-bedrock wells can produce very different results on neighboring parcels. A dry hole or low-yield result remains possible even where nearby records look good. Confirm the permitted use, construction details, pump yield, static water level, casing, and grout. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan may be required for the intended use; do not assume a permit alone settles that question.

Environmental review also deserves attention. Within about 10 miles are 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,056 historic mine features, and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not automatically mean a parcel's water is contaminated, but they justify laboratory testing and a review of site history. Keep the well and septic system separated as required by the applicable design and permitting rules, and verify that the lot can accommodate both.

sections.heading: A practical plan for building near Breckenridge
sections.html:
Before closing, obtain the Colorado DWR permit and every available construction, yield, and water-level record for the property. Compare those records with wells in Blue River, Frisco, Keystone, Dillon, Copper Mountain, and other nearby areas only as local context; the closest comparable well is usually more useful than a broad county average. Ask a qualified driller what the geology and access mean for depth, casing, grout, and refusal risk.

For a new build, confirm the well location, pump power, storage, trench route, septic field, driveway, and house footprint together. A domestic-use permit may not support every planned use, and larger demands can raise water-rights or augmentation issues. Budget from the full finished-system estimate, then carry a separate allowance for unusual depth, access, electrical work, testing, or a revised septic design.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Breckenridge, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported wells within five miles of Breckenridge have a median depth of 135 feet. The middle half is 80 to 207 feet, and the 90th percentile is 290 feet. Depth varies because most permits identify fractured-bedrock aquifers in mountain granite or gneiss. A nearby well helps with planning but cannot guarantee the depth on another parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Breckenridge?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite or gneiss. At the 135-foot median depth, drilling is estimated at $8,800 to $13,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,800 to $25,500. Deeper drilling, difficult access, or added site work can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Breckenridge well produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 8.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 8% are between 1 and 5. Have the specific well tested, because fractured rock can vary substantially between nearby lots.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Breckenridge?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that a particular property's water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped environmental records include 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,056 historic mine features, and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well through a qualified laboratory and review the property's history before relying on the water.

faq.q: Do I need to check water rights before building near Breckenridge?
faq.a: Yes. Most local permits are for domestic or household use, accounting for 86% of the records. A permit does not automatically authorize every planned use, and an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan. Review the DWR permit, intended use, and applicable water-rights requirements before buying land or designing a larger-demand home.
